newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China cotton JV mills fear import duties - traders.
newsitem.headline: China cotton JV mills fear import duties - traders.

text.p: Joint-venture cotton mills in China fear the government might impose duties on previously unfettered raw cotton imports and are rushing to replenish stocks, industry sources said on Tuesday.
"The mills fear it could change from a zero percent duty to a three percent import tax and a 13 percent value added tax, perhaps on January 1, 1997," said one source just returned from China.
Joint-venture mills currently import raw cotton duty free on condition that the processed product is exported.

Industry sources said they had not seen any official announcements on a change in policy, and an official from the Tax and Tariff Committee of the State Council said he had not heard of any such developments.

Cotton traders said joint-venture mills would in the meantime continue to take advantage of dips in world prices to briskly import cotton from the United States, West Africa and the Commonwealth of Independent States.

"Imports have accelerated in the past ... weeks and I expect this to continue," said another cotton trader, noting that mills were trying to evade fallout from any new import duties that may be announced.
"Mills are booking contracts now so in case new import taxes are announced later they can say the taxes don't apply to these contracts," an industry source said.
The price of cotton in China continued to hover at around 95 U.S. cents per pound, compared with more attractively priced imports at about 80 U.S. cents cost and freight, traders said.
China's cotton industry has been plagued by soaring stockpiles of domestic produce as cheaper imports are snapped up by mills anxious to make a profit.
"Mills still don't care about high stocks in China as long as they are free to import cheaper cotton," one trader said.

Traders said any implementation of import duties, which would effectively limit the flow of foreign cotton into China, was part of broader changes planned by the central government to revamp its cotton and textile sector.
Chinese cotton industry officials were due to hold a meeting on changes in national policy which would boost domestic cotton consumption, Hong Kong traders said.
One source said the meeting would be held in the northern province of Hubei, perhaps as early as next week, but this could not be confirmed.
Other traders said that any decision on import restrictions emerging from the meeting would not be unilateral, as China was unwilling to alter the existing tax haven for cotton joint ventures.
"China is also eager to join international organisations and a ban on imports would not look good," a cotton source said.

China pays farmers high procurement prices to encourage cotton planting, but planted acreage has fallen and China's latest estimate of its 1996 crop was 3.75 million to 3.90 million tonnes, down 13 percent from last year.
